summary: Defines a notation for describing protocol layers in a protocol encapsulation, for encoding INDEX values for the protocolDirTable in the RMON-2 MIB. It is on the standards track at the draft standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: RMON-2 needs a standard way to identify the protocols wrapped around a packet. RFC 2895 defines how to encode those layers and how textual protocol descriptions specify the encoding.

subtitle: How RMON-2 encodes protocol stacks as identifiers for its protocol directory.

tldr.problem: An RMON-2 probe needs a consistent index for each protocol encapsulation it measures, including the sequence of protocols that wrap a packet.
tldr.mechanism: Each protocol layer contributes a four-octet identifier, ordered from the base layer upward. A parallel parameter string has one octet per layer, and PI macros describe how identifiers are formed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2895 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2074 and is updated by RFC 3395. The protocol macro collection was moved to RFC 2896.

today: RFC 2895 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2074 and has been updated by RFC 3395. Its separate macro collection is in RFC 2896.

sections.title: Purpose of the Protocol Identifier
sections.content:
The RMON-2 protocol directory uses encoded identifiers to distinguish protocol encapsulations. RFC 2895 defines the encoding rules and base-layer identifiers used to build those table indexes.

The former protocol identifier document was split: this standards-track reference defines the rules, while RFC 2896 contains a separate collection of protocol macros. The document does not define an RMON MIB module itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A network monitor needs a consistent label for each protocol stack it records. This RFC defines how those labels are encoded; a companion document lists many protocol examples.

sections.title: Layers and Protocol Identifier Macros
sections.content:
A layer-identifier represents one encapsulation layer and is exactly four octets. A protocol-identifier string joins these identifiers from left to right, beginning with a base layer and continuing through its child protocols.

A protocol-identifier macro is a textual description of a protocol name, encoding, possible children, parameters, and attributes. The word “macro” is historical; these descriptions are not macros executed by a program.
sections.plainLanguage: Each layer has a four-octet identifier. Joining the identifiers in order describes the sequence of protocol layers around a packet.

sections.title: Encoding the Directory Index
sections.content:
The protocol directory index combines two OCTET STRING values: protocolDirID and protocolDirParameters. Each layer adds four octets to protocolDirID and one parameter octet to protocolDirParameters.

The identifier must include its base layer, and layers cannot be skipped. When represented in the table index, each string has a length field; the parameter string must contain exactly one quarter as many octets as protocolDirID.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier has four octets for every layer, and its companion parameter string has one octet for each layer. The first identifier must name the base layer, and the sequence cannot skip a layer.

sections.title: The Protocol Identifier Macro Format
sections.content:
The PI language uses clauses such as PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER, PARAMETERS, ATTRIBUTES, DESCRIPTION, CHILDREN, ADDRESS-FORMAT, DECODING, and REFERENCE. The RFC defines a grammar for these declarations.

Protocol names contain 1 to 64 permitted characters. Every declaration must include PARAMETERS, ATTRIBUTES, and DESCRIPTION; other clauses are required when the selected attributes say they apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A PI macro is a small structured description of a protocol. Its required clauses identify the protocol, describe it, and list its parameters and attributes.

sections.title: Parameters and Capability Attributes
sections.content:
The parameter octet lets an RMON manager request optional probe work, such as counting fragments or tracking sessions that change ports. A probe may support a parameter always, never, or depending on its available resources.

Attribute bits describe capabilities, including whether a protocol can have child layers and whether it supports address recognition. Reserved and unused bits are set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Parameter bits tell the probe which optional tracking work to perform. Attribute bits describe what the protocol and probe can support.

sections.title: Base Layers and Wildcard Identifiers
sections.content:
The base identifier is four octets: a function code, two operands, and a base-layer value. Function zero means no special function; function one is a wildcard that can aggregate counters across base encapsulations.

The RFC defines five base-layer values: ether2, llc, snap, vsnap, and ianaAssigned. The ianaAssigned layer is for protocols that cannot be identified through the usual hierarchical encapsulation rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The first identifier names the packet's base encapsulation and may request wildcard counting. RFC 2895 defines five base layers for building a complete protocol identifier.

sections.title: Relationship to ATM and Other MIBs
sections.content:
The RFC defines no dedicated base-layer macros for ATM encapsulations. A probe maps those packets onto LLC, SNAP, or vendor SNAP as appropriate; management software can use interface information to recover some additional details.

For RMON-2 counters, ATM probes count the AAL-5 frame size, not the payload size or the encapsulated MAC frame size. This identifier reference is intended for the RMON protocol directory, not other MIBs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC maps ATM traffic onto existing base layers instead of defining new ones. It also specifies which frame size RMON-2 uses for its octet counters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC concerns the syntax and meaning of textual protocol descriptions, not the definition of network behavior. It states that it raises no security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines protocol labels rather than network behavior. It reports no security considerations.
